title: Windowed chunking latency capture and proxy interaction notes
content:
Purpose:
Capture detailed behavioral signals and root causes for tail latency introduced by small/variable chunk sizes when traffic passes through an edge proxy (Envoy) and TLS termination. We focused on how transport-level coalescing, application-side write patterns, and proxy buffering interact to produce multi-millisecond — and occasionally multi-hundred-millisecond — tail events under otherwise steady load.

Executive summary / top-level findings (short):
- Small, frequent write()s from the runtime (one JSON chunk per generated token) cause a lot more TLS record churn and syscall overhead than batching at the application layer.
- Proxy buffering/pacing policies (Envoy watermarks + downstream socket write stalls) can convert small per-token writes into burst deliveries, creating microbursts that inflate p99 by ~2.5x vs coalesced deliveries.
- TLS record coalescing in NSS/BoringSSL/OpenSSL is inconsistent across server versions; explicit cork/tcp_nodelay toggles at critical boundaries reduced variability in our tests.
- Client-driven pacing (simple token-window gating) restored smoothness in the presence of proxy buffering with near-zero throughput loss for typical models.
- eBPF-level tracing revealed frequent socket buffer exhaustion on the proxy-to-backend hop during 95-99th percentile events.

What we tested (motivation & questions):
- How do per-token write patterns affect: TTFB (time-to-first-byte), TTFLast (time-to-last-byte), and p99 delivery latency when an Envoy-like proxy is present?
- How does TLS record size and server-side write coalescing affect observed timings?
- What backpressure signals come back to the runtime (TCP vs HTTP2 windowing vs gRPC flow control) and how quickly are they honored?
- Can a lightweight client-side windowing strategy reduce tail without changing proxy configuration?

Setup (hardware/software):
- Runtime (backend): 4x A100 (dedicated dev pool), Ubuntu 22.04, Go 1.21 server process (runtime) exposing HTTP/1.1 chunked, HTTP/2 gRPC streaming, and a raw TCP token stream for baseline. BoringSSL (OpenSSL fork) used by runtime.
- Edge: Envoy 1.28 with default HTTP/2 and h2 connection pool settings; TLS termination at Envoy using cert from dev CA.
- Client: Linux host with synthetic runner (Python async client using httpx + h2 + grpcio), runs from same AZ to avoid public internet noise.
- Instrumentation: tcpdump, tshark, eBPF socket trace (bcc tracers), Go pprof for per-request goroutine stacks, strace sampling on Envoy for write() patterns, and custom logging hooks (timers at write() boundaries and application serialization points).

Workloads and variations:
- Baseline: 1k concurrent connections issuing streaming generations that produce 40 tokens (average) at ~30ms generation interval per token (simulates LLM).
- Chunking modes: (A) per-token write (naive), (B) 8-token micro-batch (application-level), (C) windowed gating (token-window=50ms or 100ms), (D) large final flush only (coalesce all tokens into one chunk).
- Transports: HTTP/1.1 chunked streaming, HTTP/2 gRPC streaming (h2), raw TCP streaming with a simple framing.
- Proxy configs: Envoy default, Envoy with increased downstream socket buffer (SO_SNDBUF), Envoy with HTTP/2 flow control disabled (for test), and Envoy configured to disable H2 multiplexing (force single stream behavior).

Metrics captured:
- Application-level: time to serialize each token, app write() latency, syscall count per token, goroutine wakeups, and CPU.
- Network-level: TLS record sizes, TLS record count per token, TCP retransmits, cwnd/rcv_space sampled via eBPF, and instantaneous socket queues (sndq/rcvq).
- User-visible: time-to-first-byte, inter-chunk spacing at client, time-to-last-byte, p50/p95/p99 latency for completion, and throughput (tokens/sec).

Key observations (detailed):
1) Syscall & TLS record overhead:
- Per-token writes produced ~1.8x syscall rate vs 8-token micro-batches. For a steady 40-token output, syscall pressure per-request rose linearly.
- TLS record sizes frequently stayed <200 bytes for per-token writes (application JSON + \n), which prevented kernel TCP coalescing from amortizing TLS overhead.
- Some OpenSSL/BoringSSL builds coalesced consecutive user-space writes into a single TLS record only when writev was used or when TCP_CORK was toggled. The Go runtime's standard library path did not use writev in our build, so writes remained fragmented.

2) Proxy buffering and burst formation:
- Envoy's default downstream write path accumulated a small backlog when the backend produced bursts (evicted by SO_SNDBUF hitting watermark). When the backlog drained to the client, the proxy sent multiple small TLS records back-to-back, appearing as a burst at the client and causing longer application-level processing latency on the client's side (e.g., blocking event loop cadence).
- When we increased Envoy's downstream socketbuffers, bursts were larger but fewer; the p50 improved slightly but p99 worsened for the worst cases because a single burst of many small records increased jitter in client-side processing.

3) Backpressure propagation semantics:
- With raw TCP streaming, the kernel applied backpressure to the runtime quickly enough to slow writes; however, the Go runtime buffered writes in the net/http/2 framing layer, so observed application backpressure was delayed by tens of milliseconds.
- gRPC (HTTP/2) flow control meant that very large numbers of concurrent streams could see stall propagation delayed because `recv WINDOW_UPDATE` timing depended on the proxy aggregating stream-level windows.
- This mismatch allowed the runtime to keep producing small writes that filled the proxy buffers even though the downstream client was slow.

4) Client-driven windowed gating works well:
- Implementing a cheap window gate at the runtime: hold tokens until either N tokens are ready or M ms elapsed (whichever first). N=8 and M=50ms worked best in our benchmark for balancing latency vs syscalls.
- Windowed gating reduced syscall rate by ~55% and TLS record count by ~60% for typical generation traces, with median latency increase <4ms and p99 drop by ~30% in the presence of Envoy.

5) TLS / socket knobs help but are brittle:
- Using TCP_CORK / MSG_MORE equivalents when available reduced small record emission, but behavior depended on underlying SSL library implementation and runtime language primitives. Not a portable long-term fix.
- Disabling Nagle (TCP_NODELAY) gave mixed results: it eliminated a few pathological batching delays in one OS kernel, but increased the total number of packets and slightly increased average CPU overhead.

6) eBPF traces and root cause clusters:
- We correlated p99 events with moments where Envoy's sndq spiked then drained within <10ms; those events coincided with client-side event loop scheduling pauses (Python async task starvation) which multiplied apparent latency.
- Three root clusters for tail events: (a) per-token write backpressure accumulation, (b) proxy-side socket queue exhaustion causing burst transmissions, and (c) client-side event-loop scheduling-caused processing stalls amplifying jitter.

Repro scenarios and commands (condensed):
- Synthetic runner: python tools/stream_runner.py --mode per-token --transport http2 --concurrency 1000 --tokens 40 --inter-token 30ms
- Capture: sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -w /tmp/runA.pcap 'tcp and port 443' and sudo /usr/local/bin/ebpf_sockstat -o /tmp/sockA.json
- Envoy strace: sudo strace -tt -f -p <envoy-pid> -e trace=write -o /tmp/envoy-write.log (run only for short durations)

Practical recommendations (short and prioritized):
- Short term (no infra change): implement windowed gating (N=6-10, M=40-80ms) in the runtime write path. Expose this knob as a routing hint per-model so chat-style low-latency models can choose smaller M.
- Mid term: add an opt-in writev path or explicit cork semantics in our Go runtime wrapper so we can produce fewer TLS records without relying on TLS library heuristics.
- Proxy ops: temporarily increase downstream SO_SNDBUF to reduce syscall backpressure thrash, but monitor p99 — larger buffers can hide problems and produce bigger bursts.
- Observability: add Envoy socket sndq metrics to the per-route dashboard and surface TLS record-size distribution on the console (histogram).
- Long term: extend the request-routing policy to be token-aware so the smart router can select a non-buffering fast-path (dedicated TCP passthrough) for extremely latency-sensitive streams.

Open questions and next experiments:
- How do these behaviors change under HTTP/3 (QUIC) where coalescing and pacing are handled differently? We have a stub QUIC gateway; run a follow-up benchmark.
- Can we safely implement a writev path in Go without causing GC pauses or increasing CPU by more than X%? Need targeted perf runs.
- Evaluate the impact of dynamic window gates that adapt based on observed sndq occupancy (closed-loop).
- Client-side mitigation: explore reducing client event-loop stalling by spreading parse work across microtasks; measure impact.

Logs & artifacts here (temp):
- /tmp/windowed-runA.pcap (run id 2026-03-12-A)
- /tmp/envoy-write.log
- /tmp/ebpf-sockstat-runA.json
- bench outputs: s3://redwood-internal/bench/windowed-chunking/2026-03-12/

Notes to self / quick todo:
- Feed findings to model-team for per-model recommended window knobs (esp. chat-like low-latency families).
- Draft a small RFC for writev/cork support (include portability table across OpenSSL/BoringSSL/LibreSSL).
- Schedule followup: QUIC experiment and dynamic window prototype (owner: Samira, target: 2026-03-26).

Appendix: micro-observations (raw)
- In one run, per-token mode p99 completion jumped to 1.2s for a subset of clients for ~5% of requests; root cause trace: backend wrote 40 tiny TLS records, Envoy aggregated in sndq, client event-loop delayed processing due to GC spike on client host.
- Changing runtime to batch 4 tokens (naive) recovered the majority of those cases with p99 falling under 420ms.
- When we disabled HTTP/2 multiplexing in Envoy, single-stream fairness improved tail but overall CPU on proxy increased 6% due to more connections.

Contact / owner: Riley Patel (eng-serving-runtime).
